question: Can supervised estimation, generative modeling, active data selection, and reinforcement learning be organized as stationary paths of learning actions analogous to Fermat, Euler-Lagrange, and Hamiltonian principles?

key_findings.claim: Author proposal: information content acts as position, token surprisal as velocity, and the change in surprisal as acceleration, motivating a least-time view of sample-efficient learning.
key_findings.evidence: The paper defines cumulative Shannon information as minus log sequence probability and uses the chain rule to identify each next-token negative log probability with a discrete velocity. It then calls the token-to-token change in surprisal acceleration and hypothesizes that learning is generally decelerating because loss is bounded below and typically non-increasing. Figure 1 shows average in-context loss and its difference on OpenWebText, but this descriptive analogy does not establish a physical law or monotonicity for individual sequences, optimization trajectories, or generalization error.

key_findings.claim: Author derivation: minimizing observations to a target error under a highly symmetric linear-regression model recovers A-optimal experimental design.
key_findings.evidence: For unit-norm observations, uniformly spherical test covariates, n at least p, and ordinary least squares, the generalization error depends on trace((X-transpose X)^-1). Convexity makes the optimum isotropic with all eigenvalues n/p, producing error sigma-squared plus sigma-squared p/n. The author correctly identifies this as a special case of established A-optimality, and notes that maintaining exact isotropy generally requires planning additions in blocks of p rather than greedily adding one point.

key_findings.claim: Author derivation, explicitly not claimed as novel: stationarity of a constrained deterministic-control Lagrangian recovers the Bellman optimality equation.
key_findings.evidence: State-transition constraints are introduced with multipliers, yielding a discrete Hamiltonian composed of reward plus multiplier-weighted dynamics. Stationarity gives the costate recursion and action maximization; identifying the multiplier with the value gradient recovers deterministic Bellman recursion, then expectation extends it to stochastic transitions. This is a standard optimal-control derivation and depends on the reward hypothesis rather than deriving rewards from the proposed generalization-error action.

anchors.section: Section 3.2, RL setup and novelty disclaimer

key_findings.claim: Author postulation: a Fisher-weighted loss-field Lagrangian yields maximum likelihood as its stationary condition and is then associated with an inverse-square-root-Fisher parameter velocity.
key_findings.evidence: The proposed density is (1/2P) grad(loss)-transpose F^-1 grad(loss) minus log likelihood. Applying a scalar-field Euler-Lagrange equation and the identity E[Hessian log likelihood] = -F makes the stated stationary equation hold at maximum-likelihood critical points. The paper then equates its kinetic term to particle dynamics to write parameter velocity as F^-1/2 times the gradient. This is a postulated construction selected to reproduce known identities; it does not prove that statistical learning trajectories minimize or make this action stationary.

key_findings.claim: Reviewer contradiction: recovering an Adam-shaped denominator is not a first-principles derivation of the Adam algorithm.
key_findings.evidence: The proposed flow uses a full model Fisher and an instantaneous gradient, whereas Adam uses exponential first- and second-moment accumulators, elementwise square roots, bias corrections, numerical epsilon, and a time-varying stochastic objective. The paper lists those Adam equations only after asserting the analogy; its action does not derive beta1, beta2, bias correction, diagonalization, stochastic sampling, or the distinction between true and empirical Fisher. Moreover, standard natural gradient uses F^-1, while inverse square root requires a separate justification.

key_findings.claim: Reviewer scope audit: the claimed unification is presently a conceptual program, not a validated predictive theory of efficient learning.
key_findings.evidence: The three sections recover an established optimal-design solution, a textbook Bellman derivation, and a postulated Fisher geometry selected to resemble adaptive optimization. They do not share one empirically measured action, and no algorithm derived uniquely from the framework is benchmarked against alternatives. The conclusion itself calls experimental verification the natural next step; the only empirical graphic is a descriptive in-context-loss curve without enough protocol detail to test the broader claims.

anchors.section: Three approaches to unknown generalization error

method.core_idea: Construct learning analogues of physical least-time, Lagrangian, and Hamiltonian principles, then show that stationary conditions reproduce selected established algorithms or design criteria.
method.mechanism: Map cumulative surprisal to distance; define time-to-error as a path functional over observed data; solve a symmetric linear-regression design problem; impose dynamics with Lagrange multipliers to recover Bellman recursion; and postulate a Fisher-weighted action density for likelihood fields whose particle interpretation resembles inverse-root-Fisher adaptive updates.
assumptions: Learning progress can be represented by a sufficiently regular, generally non-increasing generalization-error or loss path.
Samples have comparable information content when sample count is interpreted as physical time.
The linear-regression example has unit-norm design points, uniformly spherical test covariates, homoscedastic noise, n at least p, and full-rank X-transpose X.
The RL derivation assumes Markov state dynamics, additive scalar reward, and the reward hypothesis; deterministic transitions are treated before an expectation-based extension.
Likelihood regularity makes the expected Hessian equal minus Fisher and an unbiased efficient-estimation interpretation is applicable.
The postulated loss-field density and the subsequent particle kinetic energy are legitimate descriptions of learning rather than merely analogical constructions.

techniques.role: Relate chain-rule surprisal to discrete position, velocity, and acceleration.
Express samples-to-error as an action-like path objective.
Solve the tractable isotropic linear-regression data-selection example.
Use multipliers, costates, and a Hamiltonian to recover Bellman recursion.
Build a likelihood-field kinetic term from inverse Fisher information.
Derive conditions intended to connect the postulated action with familiar optimizers.

evaluations.setting: Small language models evaluated in context on OpenWebText
evaluations.metric: Expected per-token negative log likelihood and its discrete first difference
evaluations.result: Figure 1 qualitatively shows decreasing loss and a diminishing improvement pattern described as information deceleration.
evaluations.baseline: No model identities, confidence intervals, intervention, or competing kinematic hypothesis are specified in the main text.

evaluations.setting: Analytic p-dimensional homoscedastic linear regression with spherical covariates
evaluations.metric: Minimum generalization error at fixed sample count and samples required for a target error
evaluations.result: The isotropic information matrix attains sigma-squared plus sigma-squared p/n; p and 2p samples yield the paper's two illustrative thresholds.
evaluations.baseline: A-optimality from classical optimal experimental design, which the authors acknowledge is the recovered known result.

evaluations.metric: Symbolic recovery of Bellman and Adam/RMSprop-shaped equations
evaluations.result: Bellman recursion is recovered exactly under the stated control setup; only an inverse-root-Fisher resemblance to adaptive optimization is obtained for Adam/RMSprop.
evaluations.baseline: Textbook optimal control and published optimizer definitions; no numerical optimizer or RL experiment.

limitations: Author-acknowledged: the manuscript is a work in progress and says its hypotheses require experimental verification.
Author-acknowledged: exact generalization error is unknown before choosing a setup and algorithm, motivating three different substitutes rather than one operational action.
Reviewer-identified: monotone bounded loss is assumed as a generic property despite stochastic training, overfitting, distribution shift, and per-example in-context loss violating monotonicity.
Reviewer-identified: the Bellman derivation is standard control theory and does not validate the novel likelihood-field action.
Reviewer-identified: the Adam analogy leaves its defining moment state, diagonal empirical statistics, bias corrections, and stochastic discretization underived.
Reviewer-identified: true Fisher, empirical Fisher, squared-gradient moving averages, F^-1 natural gradients, and F^-1/2 preconditioning are materially different objects.
Reviewer-identified: no newly predicted algorithm, falsifiable quantitative law, sample-efficiency benchmark, or realistic experimental comparison is provided.
Reviewer-identified: calling reward-Hamiltonian RL a Legendre transform of parameter estimation is asserted without an explicit invertible transform connecting the two problem classes.
failure_modes: A stationary action can be a maximum or saddle rather than a minimum-time or efficient-learning solution.
Different Lagrangians can share the same stationary trajectories, making post-hoc recovery of a known equation non-identifying.
When samples carry unequal information, observation count is not a coherent time coordinate and active selection costs matter.
Empirical Fisher can be a poor curvature proxy away from model fit, so treating Adam's accumulator as Fisher can misdiagnose its behavior.
Reward misspecification breaks the claimed link between Bellman optimality and improvement in generalization or intelligence.
Singular or poorly conditioned Fisher matrices make the proposed inverse-square-root velocity undefined or unstable without damping and approximation choices.
reusable_insights: Samples-to-threshold and wall-clock-to-threshold should be reported separately; parallel compute can reduce the latter without improving the former.
Optimal data collection can require blockwise lookahead even when every fixed-budget design has a closed-form isotropic optimum.
Lagrangian analogies become scientifically useful when they yield prospective invariants, phase-space constraints, or algorithms not inserted into the action by construction.
Any Fisher-based optimizer derivation should state whether it uses model Fisher, empirical Fisher, generalized Gauss-Newton, or a moving squared-gradient statistic.
Recovering Bellman equations via costates is a useful bridge between optimal control and RL, but reward adequacy remains an independent modeling question.
open_questions: Can one specify a single measurable learning action that applies across data selection, parameter updates, and policy optimization without changing its primitives between paradigms?
Which prospective experiment would distinguish stationary-action learning from ordinary optimal design, control, or optimizer geometry?
Can the framework derive Adam's moment recursions and hyperparameters uniquely, or does it instead predict a different implementable optimizer?
How should information-weighted time account for variable sample informativeness, acquisition cost, replay, augmentation, and parallel batches?
Can a non-monotone stochastic loss path still admit a useful action whose extremals predict sample efficiency and generalization?
What exact Legendre dual variables and convexity conditions connect likelihood parameter estimation to reward-based RL?

competitive_landscape.title: Least Action Principles and Well-Posed Learning Problems
competitive_landscape.difference: Betti and Gori formulate least cognitive action for temporal perception, prove existence for a special action, derive fourth-order learning equations, and analyze dissipation. Guo and Schölkopf seek a broader cross-paradigm analogy but do not discuss that prior least-action learning line or prove well-posedness of their postulated field action.

competitive_landscape.title: A Principle of Least Action for the Training of Neural Networks
competitive_landscape.difference: Karkar et al. treat a network as a dynamical transport system, connect low kinetic-energy displacement to generalization, derive regularity with optimal transport, and propose an algorithm. The present manuscript instead postulates an action in loss/parameter space and recovers familiar methods without comparable algorithmic or empirical validation.

competitive_landscape.title: Dissecting Adam: The Sign, Magnitude and Variance of Stochastic Gradients
competitive_landscape.difference: Balles and Hennig empirically decompose Adam and explicitly warn that the empirical-Fisher interpretation is problematic because Adam divides by the square root rather than the Fisher itself. That directly qualifies the manuscript's claim that inverse-root-Fisher dynamics amount to deriving Adam from its Lagrangian.

competitive_landscape.title: Limitations of the Empirical Fisher Approximation for Natural Gradient Descent
competitive_landscape.difference: Kunstner et al. show that empirical Fisher generally lacks the second-order meaning of model Fisher and can be pathological even on simple problems. The manuscript moves between Fisher and Adam's empirical squared-gradient statistics without treating those conditions, so its optimizer interpretation needs this distinction.

competitive_landscape.title: Fishers for Free? Approximating the Fisher Information Matrix by Recycling the Squared Gradient Accumulator
competitive_landscape.difference: Li et al. directly test when Adam-like squared-gradient accumulators approximate Fisher diagonals across five applications and quantify their differences. This supplies the kind of empirical and definitional audit absent from the manuscript's assertion that Adam approximates its Fisher-based motion.

competitive_landscape.title: Fisher Information and Natural Gradient Learning in Random Deep Networks
competitive_landscape.difference: Amari et al. start from Fisher's Riemannian metric, analyze its block structure in random deep networks, and derive an explicit approximate inverse natural gradient. The manuscript instead selects an inverse-square-root kinetic term and asserts an Adam connection without an equivalent structural approximation or convergence analysis.

novelty_assessment.author_claim: Learning-by-stationarity unifies efficient data selection, reinforcement learning, supervised learning, and generative modeling; the proposed learning Lagrangian recovers A-optimality, Bellman equations, and Adam/RMSprop-like optimization.
novelty_assessment.evidence: The manuscript provides an analytic isotropic-design calculation, a textbook discrete-control derivation, and an Euler-Lagrange calculation for a newly postulated Fisher-weighted likelihood field, plus a descriptive in-context-loss plot.
novelty_assessment.reviewer_inference: The cross-paradigm presentation and particular loss-field density are novel as exposition, but least-action learning, variational neural training, Fisher geometry, A-optimality, Bellman stationarity, and Adam-Fisher analogies all have substantial prior literature. Because the action changes interpretation across sections, known equations are largely recovered by construction, and no novel quantitative prediction is tested, this is best treated as a speculative research program rather than a first-principles unification already supported by evidence.

reviewer_notes: All 12 extracted pages were reviewed, including the derivations and references. Current neighboring work was checked on arXiv and official PMLR pages on 2026-08-23. The audit preserves the paper's explicit distinction between textbook Bellman material and its novel postulation, and flags where 'derive Adam' exceeds what the displayed equations establish.
